title: Rule from Damascus
hook: Mu'awiyah rules from Damascus, and the caliphate becomes a dynasty

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hasan's peace. A grandson of the Prophet stepped aside rather than add to the graves. Your line was peace between two groups.

Medina had been the center. The Prophet, peace be upon him, was buried there. Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman had led from there. Ali had moved to Kufa, in Iraq. And now the seat of the Muslim community moves again, north, to an old city: Damascus. The man ruling from there is Mu'awiyah, who had governed Syria under the earlier caliphs. With him, the question that had split the believers since the day after the Prophet's death takes a new shape. Not only who should lead, but how leadership passes on.
screen: `MEDINA, THEN KUFA.` → `NOW DAMASCUS.` → `HOW DOES LEADERSHIP PASS ON?`

segments.voice: Each caliph so far had come to office a different way. Abu Bakr by a pledge in a meeting hall. Umar named by Abu Bakr. Uthman chosen by a council. Ali by a pledge in the mosque, in a crisis. None was a son taking over from a father. The histories report that in his later years Mu'awiyah asked the people to pledge loyalty, in advance, to his son Yazid. Some refused; several sons of the great companions in Medina are reported among them, and so is Husayn. But the pledge was taken, and when Mu'awiyah died, Yazid ruled. The rule of one family, the Umayyads, had begun, passing from father to son, or cousin to cousin, for generations. A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi says that the caliphate of prophethood would last thirty years, and after it God would give kingship to whom He wills. In Arabic, the word for that kingship is mulk. Some scholars read that hadith against this very moment. Sunni and Shia Muslims see Mu'awiyah differently. Sunni Muslims count him a companion of the Prophet, and Sunni teaching gives him the respect owed to companions, while some Sunni scholars are frank that turning the caliphate into an inheritance was a change for the worse. Shia Muslims see him as the man who fought Ali, the rightful Imam, and who set the stage for the tragedy that came next. Either way, a community that had chosen its leaders now inherited them.
screen: `FOUR CALIPHS, FOUR WAYS IN.` · `A PLEDGE FOR YAZID, IN ADVANCE.` · `CALIPHATE, THEN KINGSHIP.` · `SUNNI AND SHIA SEE HIM DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `A DYNASTY BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something handed down to you that you didn't choose: a family business, a role, a name, a way of doing things, even a grudge. Ask which parts came to you because they were right, and which only because they were yours. Then think of one thing you will hand on, and how it could pass fairly.
Mulk, kingship: the hadith's word for the rule God gives after the caliphate of prophethood, the moment Mu'awiyah's rule began to pass from father to son. Today's word.
Your line: a dynasty begins. It would run for generations. Day eight hundred eighty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Muslims remember the move of the caliphate to Damascus under Mu'awiyah as the start of the Umayyad dynasty; Sunni Muslims honor him as a companion while often criticizing the hereditary turn, and Shia Muslims remember him as Ali's opponent.

chat.says: What changed when Mu'awiyah's son Yazid took over?
options: Rule became inherited, passed within one family, the Umayyads.
Nothing new; every caliph before him was a caliph's son.
The caliphs began to be chosen by a vote in Damascus.
chat.meaning: Earlier caliphs came by pledge, nomination or council; none was a son succeeding his father. With Yazid, the Umayyad family's inherited rule began.

Damascus.meaning: an old city in Syria, Mu'awiyah's seat

Yazid.meaning: Mu'awiyah's son, pledged to in advance

Umayyads.meaning: Mu'awiyah's family, who ruled for generations

Abu Dawud.meaning: compiler of a major hadith collection
